newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran presidential hopefuls get message across.
newsitem.headline: Iran presidential hopefuls get message across.

text.p: Fighting for key votes in Iran's presidential election on Friday is helped when your campaign is taken to the streets by the Islamic Republic's national weightlifting and martial arts squad.

That is what parliamentary speaker and presidential hopeful Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri is doing to win over 500,000 voters who live in one of largest wards in this crowded city of around seven million people.

Nateq-Nouri's campaign centre in Tehran's middle class District Two is based in a modern gym complete with bench-presses, weights and cycle machines and is led by four heavy-set, monied supporters, some of whom have doubled as security guards for the cleric.

"This is Mr Nateq-Nouri's main campaign office for this district, and it is run by the Society of Combatant Clerics and the Society of Athletes," said Davood Asghari, a martial arts expert whose business card shows a picture of him bare-chested in a karate high-kick.

Asghari's smart suit and mobile phone contrast with the district headquarters of Nateq-Nouri's main challenger Mohammad Khatami, a former culture and guidance minister, which operates out of a down-at-heel office just a km away.
Khatami's supporters work and sleep in a rented office surrounded by pots of glue and ladders needed to paste up posters of their candidate on walls in the district.

The election campaign here for the last two months has involved getting people to go to Khatami's lectures and to invite sympathetic parliament members to speak in local mosques, the public liaison officer at the office said.
Unlike Asghari's team equipped with electronic pagers and Persian carpets, Khatami's make do with a single radio and telephone line, and the television is broken.

A third presidential hopeful, former intelligence (internal security) minister Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri, has his offices in a modest converted shop in west Tehran where a solitary supporter, Mehdi Goljan of the Society for Defence of the Values of the Islamic Revolution, offers leaflets and posters.
The only non-cleric to run in the race, deputy head of judiciary Reza Zavarei, drums up support through posters and television and radio time allocated equally to all candidates.
The four candidates are vying to succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani who has served the maximum two four-year terms allowed under Iran's Islamic constitution.

According to one locally published opinion poll, Nateq- Nouri has an edge over Khatami though the latter's support particularly amongst many of Tehran's large young population has increased voter interest in the election.
"Khatami's appeal to the young people has created a shockwave in society...The young are brighter and more up to date and have more demands," said the liaison officer.
"Freedom of expression is the common point between Islam and liberalism...What we are looking for is a religious goverment not a governmental religion," he added.

Two male university students, Mohsen and Hamid, walking down the street near Khatami's office said they would vote for him because they thought he would ease dress restrictions on campus and allow access to satellite television which is now outlawed.

Nateq-Nouri's weightlifting campaigners promote their candidate as the most experienced of the runners and the one who will totally obey the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and will show no inclination to the West.

"He fights (Western) arrogance and has been touched by poverty...He is committed to Islamic values and principles...He is a man of action," is the message that Asghari and his three gym colleagues take to the streets of Tehran District Two.
